idiom_name: Map<String, Object> attribute map behind named accessors
implementation_notes: There is no dynamic member access in the language, so the owner carries a Map<String, Object> (or Map<AttributeKey<?>, Object> when keys must be typed) behind get/set/remove/has methods, and a key-set accessor gives discovery. java.util.Properties is the JDK's String-to-String property list, and java.beans.Introspector with PropertyDescriptor supplies the descriptor participant - type, read/write methods, display names - but only for statically declared bean properties, so per-instance additions are invisible to JavaBeans tooling unless a DynaBean-style bridge is used. Classic structure is hand-written, and it is the right call whenever the keys are data rather than a fixed API; use Commons BeanUtils when other tooling must see the dynamic properties as JavaBeans.
pitfalls: Every read is an unchecked cast; a value stored under the wrong key type surfaces as ClassCastException far from the write site, and a typo'd key just returns empty. Typed key objects (Map<AttributeKey<?>, Object>, Fowler's Defined/Typed Dynamic Property) move that failure to the boundary.
java.beans.Introspector caches BeanInfo per class, so dynamically generated or reloaded classes need Introspector.flushCaches()/flushFromCaches() or their new properties stay invisible.

Introspector and PropertyDescriptor describe declared getters and setters only - per-instance additions need a DynaBean or an ICustomTypeDescriptor-style bridge before JavaBeans consumers can see them.
java.util.Properties is Hashtable-based, synchronized and String-to-String only; it is a configuration store, not a general property bag.

variants.name: DynaBean / DynaClass (Apache Commons BeanUtils)
variants.implementation_notes: BeanUtils supplies the full structure for beans whose properties are not declared in code: a DynaBean supports properties whose names and data types, as well as their values, may be dynamically modified, LazyDynaBean adds a property to its class when set(name, value) first sees it, and DynaClass is the runtime descriptor set (the pattern's PropertyType/Descriptors) that tooling can enumerate. Choose it when frameworks, expression languages or data binders insist on JavaBeans-shaped access; prefer a plain Map when only your own code reads the properties.
pitfalls: A LazyDynaBean accepts any name on set(), so a typo becomes a new property instead of an error - restrict the MutableDynaClass or validate names when input is untrusted.

DynaClass reports a property descriptor even for names that do not exist in the default configuration (getDynaProperty returns a synthetic descriptor unless setReturnNull(true)), so existence checks must use isDynaProperty(name).
DynaBean properties are not visible to java.beans.Introspector unless other BeanUtils components adapt them, and ClassCastExceptions remain the failure mode for wrong-typed values.
